title: Transactions and Best Practices in ADO.NET
description: Implement database transactions, handle errors gracefully, and follow connection management best practices.

data.text: Real-world applications often need to perform multiple database operations as a single logical unit. **Transactions** ensure that either all operations succeed or none do. Combined with proper error handling and connection management, transactions make your data access code robust and reliable.
A **transaction** is a group of one or more database operations that are executed as a single unit. A transaction has four key properties, known by the acronym **ACID**:

items: **Atomicity** — All operations succeed, or none do.
**Consistency** — The database remains in a valid state before and after the transaction.
**Isolation** — Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other.
**Durability** — Once committed, changes survive system failures.

data.caption: Transaction flow in ADO.NET
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Begin Transaction] --> B[Operation 1: INSERT]
    B --> C{Success?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Operation 2: UPDATE]
    C -->|No| E[Rollback]
    D --> F{Success?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Commit]
    F -->|No| E
    G --> H[Changes Saved]
    E --> I[All Changes Discarded]

data.text: In ADO.NET, you create a transaction by calling `BeginTransaction()` on an open `SqlConnection`. All `SqlCommand` objects created from that connection participate in the transaction until you call `Commit()` or `Rollback()`.

data.title: Transaction rules
data.text: Always call Commit() only after all operations succeed. If any command throws an exception, call Rollback() in the catch block. The transaction is automatically rolled back if the connection closes without a commit.
Database operations can fail for many reasons: network issues, constraint violations, deadlocks, or timeout. A robust data access layer handles these gracefully and provides useful feedback.

data.title: Robust Error Handling Pattern
data.content: Wrap database operations in try-catch with specific exception handling.

data.text: Proper connection management is essential for performance and scalability. Connections are a limited server resource, and poor management leads to connection pool exhaustion.

cards.title: using Statement (Recommended)
cards.description: Wraps the connection in a using block, ensuring Dispose() is called even if an exception occurs.

cards.title: Manual Close
cards.description: Explicitly calling Close() in a finally block.

cards.title: Connection Pooling
cards.description: Enabled by default. Reuses physical connections instead of creating new ones each time.

items: Always wrap SqlConnection, SqlCommand, and SqlDataReader in using statements.
Open connections as late as possible and close them as early as possible.
Use async methods (`OpenAsync`, `ExecuteReaderAsync`, etc.) for scalable web applications.
Set appropriate CommandTimeout values for long-running queries.
Log exceptions with enough context to diagnose issues (SQL, parameters, user context).
Avoid storing connection strings in source control; use user secrets or environment variables.

items.question: Do I need to call connection.Close() if I use a using statement?
items.answer: No. The using statement calls Dispose() on the connection, which implicitly closes it. The using pattern is preferred over manual Close() calls.

items.question: What happens if I forget to rollback a transaction?
items.answer: If the connection closes or the command times out without an explicit Commit or Rollback, SQL Server automatically rolls back the transaction. However, you should always call Rollback() explicitly in your catch block for clarity.

items.question: Should I use transactions for every database operation?
items.answer: No. Single INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements are atomic by default in SQL Server. Use transactions only when you need to combine multiple operations into an atomic unit.

items.question: What is the difference between Rollback and Dispose?
items.answer: Rollback explicitly undoes changes made during the transaction. Dispose cleans up the SqlTransaction object. Calling Dispose without Commit implicitly rolls back the transaction in SQL Server.

items.text: All connections, commands, and readers use using statements.
items.hint: Verify no manual Close() calls without using.

items.text: Transactions use try-catch with explicit Commit or Rollback.
items.hint: Rollback in catch, Commit only on success.

items.text: SqlException is caught separately from general Exception.
items.hint: Allows specific handling for deadlocks, timeouts, and constraint violations.

items.text: Connection strings are loaded from configuration, not hardcoded.
Async methods are used for I/O-bound operations in ASP.NET Core.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Transactions group multiple operations into an atomic unit using SqlTransaction.
Always call Commit() on success and Rollback() on failure.
using statements guarantee proper disposal of connections and commands.
Async methods improve scalability in ASP.NET Core web applications.
data.takeaway: You now have the complete ADO.NET toolkit: architecture, setup, reading, CRUD, security, and transactions. You are ready to build production-ready data access code.
